metadata.title: Grok Bot, Built: Planet Express Ship
metadata.topic: BLENDER BUILD · HOW TO BUILD IT
metadata.render_by: Professor Bear, with his own tools (beat sheet only)
metadata.display_rule: Viewers only ever see or hear 'the Liam voice'. No subtitles, no captions, no .srt. Hand-build steps are labelled as a Blender UI reconstruction.

beats.narration_text: This is Liam. This is the Planet Express ship, built by Grok Bot in Blender, entirely from Python, run headless. Fifteen rounds against twelve photos of a toy. First, walk around it. Then the real question: if you wanted to build this yourself, by hand, in Blender, how would you do it?
beats.new_visual_element: Round 15 · front three-quarter

shot.label: Round 15 · front three-quarter

beats.narration_text: The right side. The turret, four portholes, the hatch and ladder, the ribbed cream vent, the swept fin, the wing, and the engine bell. The left side is where the logo reads the right way round, as it does on the toy.
beats.new_visual_element: Side · side, left

shot.label: Side · side, left

beats.narration_text: From the front, the dark visor sits above the red lip, with a beak at the centre. From behind, the cream engine bell with its cluster of black lugs. From above, the turret, the fin root strip, the vents and the wings.
beats.new_visual_element: Front · rear three-quarter · top

shot.label: Front · rear three-quarter · top

beats.narration_text: Up close. The visor's three light-blue panes. The stepped turret with its dome and gun. Twelve big lugs around an inner ring of eight. The fin with its logo, an original drawn approximation, not the real artwork. And the riveted wing root.
beats.new_visual_element: Details: cockpit · turret · engine · fin · vent and wing

shot.label: Details: cockpit · turret · engine · fin · vent and wing

beats.narration_text: The brief was twelve photos of a toy model, from Professor Bear. Grok Bot gave every photo its own camera, matched by eye, so each round could be rendered and stacked against the photo. That's the loop for the whole build. Build, render, compare, correct.
beats.new_visual_element: Reference photo above · render below

shot.label: Reference photo above · render below

ai_did.summary: Twelve cameras in params.json, one per reference photo (target, azimuth, elevation, distance, lens); every round renders all twelve.

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Add the photos as camera Background Images (Camera properties → Background Images → Add Image).
One camera per photo; keep the photo's aspect ratio in Output properties.
Keep the photos visible at about 50% opacity while you model.

beats.narration_text: Start with the hull, because everything else sits on it. Grok Bot's script builds it as one lofted quad mesh: two hundred stations along the length, a hundred and twenty-eight points around each one, every cross-section a superellipse, driven by profile tables for the width, the lip line, the top and the bottom.
beats.new_visual_element: AI did: one lofted superellipse hull

shot.label: AI did: one lofted superellipse hull

ai_did.summary: Hull = one lofted quad mesh: nx 200 stations by nth 128 points, superellipse sections from the w / lip / top / bot profile tables.

beats.narration_text: By hand, you'd do the same idea with simpler tools. Add a cylinder, lay it along the length, and stretch it into a long egg. Add loop cuts for stations. Then scale each ring against the side and top photos, and pull the nose to a point with proportional editing. Shade smooth, and add a subdivision surface on top.
beats.new_visual_element: By hand: cylinder → loop cuts → shape to the photo

shot.label: By hand: cylinder → loop cuts → shape to the photo

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Add → Mesh → Cylinder (32 vertices); R Y 90 to lay it along X.
S X to stretch it to the hull length; Tab into Edit Mode.
Ctrl+R to add 10 to 20 loop cuts along the length.
Select each ring (Alt+click) and S, S Y, S Z to match the side and top photos.
O for proportional editing; G X on the nose ring to draw it to a point.
Object → Shade Smooth; Ctrl+2 for a Subdivision Surface.

beats.narration_text: Proportions come from references. For fourteen rounds, the tables were traced from the photos. For round fifteen, Professor Bear sent an STL kit of the ship: twenty-six printable parts. Grok Bot rotated the two hull halves into one frame and measured them slice by slice. One hundred seventy-eight point six millimetres long, plus a bell of about twenty-five. Forty-nine point four wide. Forty-eight point three high. Then it scaled the hull to point zero six six model units per millimetre.
beats.new_visual_element: Rounds 12 → 15 · round 15 refit to the STL kit

shot.label: Rounds 12 → 15 · round 15 refit to the STL kit

ai_did.summary: Round 15 refit the hull profile tables to the STL kit envelope (178.6 x 49.4 x 48.3 mm, bell ~25 mm) at 0.066 units/mm, measured with stl/measure.py.

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Scene properties → Units: Metric, Length: Millimetres (or keep one unit and write down the scale).
Import the STL parts (File → Import → STL) as a measuring guide, on their own collection.
N panel → Item → Dimensions: read the hull's length, width and height; scale your hull to match.
Hide the guide collection before rendering.

beats.narration_text: Then the parts, in the order the script builds them, which is a good order for a person too. Materials. The hull. The red lip band along the widest line. The portholes. The cockpit visor. The turret. The tail fin and its logo. The vents and hatches. The wings. The engine bell. And last, the studio. Every detail is placed on the hull's surface, so when the hull changes, the details follow it.
beats.new_visual_element: Build order: hull first, details on the surface

shot.label: Build order: hull first, details on the surface

ai_did.summary: build_pe.py sections run materials → hull → lip band → portholes → cockpit → turret → fin and logo → vents and hatches → wings → engine → studio; details are placed with surface functions of the hull.

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Model the hull and freeze it before details (save a copy: File → Save Copy).
Snapping: Face Project, with Align Rotation to Target, to set parts flush on the hull.
Or add a Shrinkwrap modifier to thin parts (lip, strips) targeting the hull.
Keep each part a separate object named for what it is.

beats.narration_text: Modifiers. Here's what the script really uses. Solidify, to give thin patches and the fin their thickness. Bevel, on the fin's edges. Subdivision surface, on the wings. And here's what it doesn't use. No mirror modifier: it builds the left and right parts in a loop, plus one side, then minus one. And no booleans. The portholes are a cream ring, a glass disc and a dark backing, sitting on the skin, not cut through it.
beats.new_visual_element: AI did: solidify · bevel · subdivision · no mirror · no boolean

shot.label: AI did: solidify · bevel · subdivision · no mirror · no boolean

ai_did.summary: Modifiers in build_pe.py: SOLIDIFY (patches, fin), BEVEL (fin, angle-limited, 3 segments), SUBSURF level 2 (wings). Sides built with `for side in (1,-1)`; no MIRROR, no BOOLEAN.

beats.narration_text: By hand, you'd lean on a mirror modifier: shape one side, get both, with clipping on so the seam stays closed. You might cut the porthole holes with a boolean, then clean up the faces. Both ways work. The script's way keeps the hull one clean surface, and that's worth copying.
beats.new_visual_element: By hand: mirror · bevel · subdivision · optional boolean

shot.label: By hand: mirror · bevel · subdivision · optional boolean

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Modifier tab → Add Modifier → Generate → Mirror; axis Y, Clipping on.
Bevel modifier: Limit Method Angle, 3 segments, small width.
Solidify on thin panels and the fin; check Even Thickness.
Optional: Boolean (Difference) with a cylinder cutter per porthole, then tidy the topology.
Subdivision Surface last in the stack.

beats.narration_text: Materials are simple glossy plastic. One principled shader per colour, set from a hex value: teal, a darker teal, cream, red, light-blue glass, black for the exhaust lugs. The teal gets a light clear coat. The logo is an image texture on the fin, mirrored on one side like the toy. Thirteen materials in all.
beats.new_visual_element: Principled BSDF per colour · logo texture

shot.label: Principled BSDF per colour · logo texture

ai_did.summary: mat() builds a Principled BSDF per params colour (base colour from hex, roughness 0.12 to 0.7); teal coat 0.25; logo.png / logo_m.png image textures.

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Material tab → New; Base Color → Hex (for example 1A9A8A); Roughness about 0.3.
Coat Weight 0.25 on the teal for the toy gloss.
Fin logo: Shader Editor → Image Texture into Base Color; UV-unwrap the fin (U → Project From View).
Assign materials per part, or per face in Edit Mode.

beats.narration_text: Lighting and cameras. Cycles, on the C P U, with the denoiser on. Four area lights: a key, a fill, a top and a rim, over a pale grey world. Every reference photo has its own camera, with a lens from fifty to a hundred millimetres. By hand, add a camera, look through it, and nudge it until the render lines up with the photo. That's what matched by eye means.
beats.new_visual_element: Cycles · four area lights · 12 matched cameras

shot.label: Cycles · four area lights · 12 matched cameras

ai_did.summary: Cycles CPU, OpenImageDenoise, 24 samples; area lights Key/Fill/Top/Rim; world #D9DADB; cameras from (target, azimuth, elevation, distance, lens 50/70/85/100 mm).

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: Render properties → Render Engine: Cycles; Denoise on.
Add → Light → Area, four times: key, fill, top, rim; point each with a Track To constraint or by hand.
World colour pale grey, strength about 0.8.
Add → Camera; Numpad 0; N panel → View → Lock Camera to View; move until the photo lines up.
Camera properties → Focal Length to match the photo's look (try 50, 85, 100 mm).

beats.narration_text: Checking against the references is the step that matters most. Every round rendered all twelve cameras and stacked each render under its photo. Silhouette overlays caught the hull height in round fourteen. A first try at twenty percent taller overshot, and was backed off to eight percent.
beats.new_visual_element: Compare sheets: photo above, render below

shot.label: Compare sheets: photo above, render below

ai_did.summary: compare.py stacks render under photo per camera; overlay.py draws silhouette overlays; round 14 height x1.20 overshot, backed off to x1.08.

beats.narration_text: Export. The script applies the modifiers and writes a G L B, the glTF binary, with the logo texture embedded. By hand, that's File, Export, glTF two point oh, format G L B, apply modifiers on. The G L B carries the shapes and flat glossy colours. The lights, cameras and render setup stay in the dot blend file.
beats.new_visual_element: File → Export → glTF 2.0 (.glb)

shot.label: File → Export → glTF 2.0 (.glb)

ai_did.summary: final.py: bpy.ops.export_scene.gltf(export_format='GLB', export_apply=True) after the gallery renders.

ui_steps.label: Blender UI reconstruction (hypothetical, not a recorded session)
steps: File → Export → glTF 2.0 (.glb/.gltf).
Format: glTF Binary (.glb).
Include: Selected Objects if needed; Data → Mesh → Apply Modifiers on.
Re-import the .glb into an empty scene to check it.

beats.narration_text: Now the rounds. Grok Bot scored round twelve four out of ten. Professor Bear said: pretty good, maybe a six out of ten, but it could use another round. He asked for a chunkier hull, a low flat visor with a V beak, the engine cluster, and the wings.
beats.new_visual_element: Round 12: Grok Bot 4/10 · Professor Bear about 6/10

shot.label: Round 12: Grok Bot 4/10 · Professor Bear about 6/10

beats.narration_text: Round thirteen fixed the visor, the beak and the engine. But it skipped the hull, and that was Grok Bot's own mistake. Its instruction for the round said keep what works, so the hull was kept. Round fourteen made the hull fuller. Round fifteen refit it to the STL kit.
beats.new_visual_element: r13 visor, beak, engine · r14 fuller hull · r15 STL refit

shot.label: r13 visor, beak, engine · r14 fuller hull · r15 STL refit

beats.narration_text: Grok Bot's score for round fifteen: five and a half out of ten. The side is the best, a six. The front is a five: next to photo six, it now looks too narrow and pointed. The rear is a four, because the engine bell is too big and sticks out too far. The top, five and a half. It's clearly the Planet Express ship. It wouldn't pass for the toy.
beats.new_visual_element: Round 15: Grok Bot 5.5/10 · side 6 · front 5 · rear 4 · top 5.5

shot.label: Round 15: Grok Bot 5.5/10 · side 6 · front 5 · rear 4 · top 5.5

beats.narration_text: Two scores, two judges. At round twelve, Grok Bot said four. Professor Bear said six. The numbers saw every gap. The human saw a ship that was nearly there, and picked the four things to fix. On round fifteen, his verdict is still pending. His eye decides the next round, not the script.
beats.new_visual_element: Professor Bear: round 15 verdict pending

shot.label: Professor Bear: round 15 verdict pending

beats.narration_text: What the evidence doesn't establish. The cameras are matched by eye, so some of the hull's extra height in the side photos may be the photos' close, wide lenses, not the model. This film can't tell you which. The small parts in the kit were named by shape and size only. And the hand steps here are a reconstruction. Nobody has built this ship by hand to test them.
beats.new_visual_element: Not established

shot.label: Not established

beats.narration_text: So, to build it yourself. One good hull first. Proportions from real measurements, not guesses. Details that sit on the surface. A camera matched to every reference. Then compare, every round. And keep a person in the loop, because the numbers can say it's close before the eye agrees.
beats.new_visual_element: Hull · measure · details on the surface · compare · a human in the loop

shot.label: Hull · measure · details on the surface · compare · a human in the loop

beats.narration_text: Grok Bot, Built. This is Liam.
